studies.title: By The Star When It Falls
studies.meaning: One oath, and then a defence phrased as three denials. He has not strayed, he is not deceived, and he does not speak from his own inclination. The word used for him is companion, which points at the audience's own long acquaintance with the man: they knew him before any of this. Then the positive statement, that what he says is revelation being sent, and the teacher is named by an attribute rather than a name.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the sources place this surah early, in the years when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was still being argued with by people who had known him all their lives. The commentators note the choice of the word companion: the objection was not that a stranger had appeared but that a familiar man was saying something new. The oath by the falling star has several readings and no reported occasion.

keyTerms.note: A verb for downward motion, used of a star setting, a thing dropping, and a bird stooping. It shares its letters with the word for inclination that appears two lines later.
Someone you keep company with, not a title of rank. Using it here appeals to what the audience already knows about his character over decades, rather than to any claim about him.
The pull of what a person wants, from the same root as the falling in the opening oath. Arabic hears wanting as a downward movement, and the surah puts both uses within three lines.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was small enough that reputation was a matter of record. A man's honesty was known from his trading, his marriages and his handling of disputes, and there was nowhere to go to escape a bad name. The audience being addressed had watched this particular man from childhood, and the sources report that his reliability was not in dispute even among those who rejected what he said.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb in the opening oath and the noun for desire three lines later come from the same three letters. One describes a star going down and the other describes what a person leans toward, so the surah's first argument turns on a root that means falling. Arabic writes both words with the same skeleton, and only the vowels and context separate them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage defends the message by first defending the man, and it does so on grounds anyone could check: not miracles, but a life the audience had observed. Then it separates the two things that could make speech unreliable, error and self-interest, and denies each. What remains is a claim about origin. The teacher is identified only by strength, which leaves the description open and prepares the account that follows.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same appeal to a lifetime spent among them before any revelation came.
Describes the bearer of the message in similar terms, strong and trusted at the throne.
Denies the same two alternatives, poet and soothsayer, and affirms a sending down.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose word you take without checking, and ask what actually earned that. It is almost never an argument. It is years of small consistencies you were not recording at the time. Then ask which people take your word that way, and what you have been doing lately that either adds to that account or quietly spends it.

studies.title: Two Bows' Length Away
studies.meaning: The classical commentators read this passage in two ways and both are transmitted from the earliest generation. On one reading the one who drew near is the angel who brought the revelation, seen in his own form at the horizon; on the other it is a nearness to God described without any physical sense. Neither reading was abandoned, and the wording supports both because it never supplies a name. The measurement given is the length of two bows, or nearer.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The sources report an early experience in which the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) saw the bearer of revelation filling the horizon, and the commentators connect these lines to it. They also record a second reading, in which the passage describes the night journey and what was disclosed then. Both readings are old, both are mainstream, and the classical works set them out beside one another.

keyTerms.note: A noun for firmness and well-made constitution, from a root for twisting a rope tight. Paired with the phrase before it, the description is of power that is stable rather than sudden.
A verb for lowering oneself, used of a bucket let down a well and of fruit hanging within reach. Placed after a verb for approaching, it makes the nearness a deliberate descent.
The distance between two points, used of the span of a bow from grip to tip. The measurement is given in the most familiar object an Arab carried, and then made smaller.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A bow was standard equipment and its length was a shared unit. Men measured distances by it the way later people used a pace or a rod, and two bows laid end to end was a specific, ordinary span that anyone could picture without being told. The commentators also record a custom in which two allies laid their bows together and drew as one, so the phrase carried a sense of closeness as well as distance.
studies.didYouKnow: The line describing what was communicated says only that He revealed to His servant what He revealed. The content is withheld, and the same construction is used twice in the surah: what covered the tree is described as what covered it. Both times the sentence names an event and refuses to say what happened inside it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records an encounter and withholds its content, which is unusual for a text that argues so much. What it establishes is that revelation came through a real event with a location, a distance and a witness, rather than through an inward impression that could not be described at all. And by leaving the identity of the one who drew near unstated, it keeps the account within the limits of what the Prophet reported, which is why the tradition preserved two readings instead of settling on one.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same encounter from another angle, seen at the clear horizon and not withheld.
Records the night journey that one classical reading connects to the second sighting here.
Sets out the ways God speaks to a human being, including from behind a veil and by a messenger.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of this passage is measurement and how little is content. Someone came near, at a stated distance, and what was said is not reported. Try telling one story from your own life that way this week: where it happened, how close you were, and nothing about what it meant. You will find out how much of your usual telling is interpretation.

studies.title: The Heart Did Not Lie
studies.meaning: The verification is placed in an organ, not in the eyes. What is denied is that the heart misreported what was seen, which means the seeing and the understanding of it are treated as one act. The commentators divide over whether the sight was with the eye or with the heart, and they record both. Then a second occasion is stated, at a named place, and the tree marks a boundary: the point past which nothing goes.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The dispute the ayah refers to was live: the sighting was being contested in Mecca, and the question form assumes an ongoing argument rather than a settled report. The classical works record two positions among the earliest authorities on what exactly was seen, one holding it was the angel and one that it was a vision of the Lord, and the major commentaries present both without resolving the question.

keyTerms.note: One of several Quranic words for the heart, from a root for glowing or burning. It names the seat of perception and recognition rather than of emotion, which is why it can be said to see.
A verb form for contending back and forth, from a root for milking, which pictures an argument drawn out until nothing is left. It implies persistence rather than a single objection.

keyTerms.gloss: the lote tree of the boundary
keyTerms.note: A named tree at a limit, from a verb meaning to come to an end. Commentators describe it as the point beyond which created knowledge does not pass, and they do not describe it further.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The lote tree was an ordinary sight in Arabia. It grew where there was water, it gave dense shade in a country with very little, its leaves were used for washing the dead, and travellers used particular trees as landmarks on a route. Naming a tree as the marker of an outer boundary used the most familiar possible object for the most remote possible place.
studies.didYouKnow: The first fifty-six ayat of this surah all end on the same long vowel, an unbroken rhyme running from the opening oath onward. The last six lines break it and never return. The shift is audible to a listener who understands no Arabic at all, and it falls exactly where the surah stops arguing and starts issuing its final warning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes an experience testable in the only way an experience can be: by the character of the person reporting it. It does not describe what was seen, and it does not offer the audience a way to see it. What it insists on is that the report is accurate, and the accuracy is located in the heart rather than in the eye, which is a claim about perception itself. Some things, it implies, are received rather than observed.

crossReferences.why: States that vision does not grasp Him while He grasps vision, which frames the whole discussion.
Locates blindness in the hearts inside the chests rather than in the eyes.
Records Moses asking to see and the answer he was given, the classical parallel here.

studies.applyIt: There is something you know that you cannot demonstrate to anyone — about a person, a decision, a moment you were alone for. Notice how you carry it: usually either by insisting, or by quietly dropping it. This passage does neither. It states the thing once, names the place, and lets the dispute continue. Try that with yours.

studies.title: The Sight Did Not Swerve
studies.meaning: Two verbs describe what the eye did not do. It did not slide off to one side and it did not go past what was there, so the report is bracketed on both sides: nothing missed and nothing added. Then the passage says he saw some of the greatest signs, not all of them, and stops. The next line turns to three names the audience used, and asks them to look at those the same way.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The three names in the last two lines belonged to shrines the region actually visited: one at Taif, one on the road to Iraq, one on the coast near Yathrib, each with custodians, offerings and pilgrim traffic. Naming them in a public recitation was not an abstract theological point. It named three functioning institutions with income and reputations attached.

keyTerms.note: A verb for turning aside from a straight line, used of a gaze sliding away and of a heart going crooked. Denying it says the looking stayed fixed on what was in front of it.
The verb used elsewhere of tyrants and of floodwater rising past its channel. Applied to eyesight it means seeing more than was there, so the denial rules out embellishment as well as error.
The preposition here is partitive, so the phrase says some of them rather than all. The limit is deliberate, and the commentators note that the passage never claims a complete disclosure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A shrine was an economy. Pilgrims arrived with animals and goods, custodian families collected and redistributed offerings, truces were declared around the visiting seasons, and whole clans took their standing from the site they kept. Attacking the standing of three of the best-known shrines in western Arabia touched the livelihoods of people the audience knew by name, which is part of why the surah's later ayat expect anger.
studies.didYouKnow: The two denials about the eyesight are the same pair of verbs the Quran uses elsewhere for moral failure: one for a heart that turns crooked and one for a person who oversteps every limit. Applied to a gaze, they turn accurate seeing into a kind of integrity, and inaccurate seeing into a kind of wrongdoing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Accuracy is treated as a moral quality here, not merely a cognitive one. The two things denied of the eyesight are the same two things the Quran denies of a sound character, so seeing rightly and being upright are described with one vocabulary. The partitive phrase then keeps the claim modest: some of the signs, not the whole. A report that stops where the experience stopped is offered as the mark of its truthfulness.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for swerving of hearts that go after what is ambiguous in the Book.
Uses the other verb of floodwater rising past its limit, the image behind overstepping.
Uses the same phrase about the greatest signs, spoken to Moses before he was sent.

studies.applyIt: Take one story you tell often and cut it back to what you can actually vouch for. Most retellings drift in the same two directions this passage rules out: leaving out the part that spoils it, and adding the part that improves it. Tell it once this week without either, and notice how much shorter and how much better it is.

studies.title: Names You Gave Them
studies.meaning: The argument is made from the audience's own valuations rather than from doctrine. In their society sons were an asset and daughters were a burden; the passage takes that as given and points out what they have done with it. Then the description of the three shrines is reduced to a single claim: they are names. Nothing was sent down about them, and what is followed instead is conjecture together with what people want, which the passage names as two separate things.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The practice of assigning daughters to God while regarding the birth of a daughter as a misfortune is documented across the Quran and in the pre-Islamic poetry, and this ayah is the sharpest statement of the inconsistency. The commentators note that the argument does not endorse the valuation it borrows; it uses the audience's own accounting to show what the arrangement implies.

keyTerms.note: A rare adjective for a share that shortchanges one side, from a verb for defrauding in a division. It occurs nowhere else in the Quran and its unusual form drew comment from the early grammarians.
From a root for power and dominance, used in the Quran for the backing that makes a claim binding. Saying none was sent down for these names denies them a licence rather than an existence.
The same root as the falling star in the surah's opening line and the inclination denied in its third. By this point the chapter has used those three letters three times.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Division was a constant practical problem. Inheritance, spoils, water rights and grazing were split between claimants, and a bad division started feuds that lasted generations. Arbitrators were called in for exactly this, and a man's reputation could rest on having divided something fairly. The word used for the arrangement in this passage is the word for a share that cheats, and everybody listening had seen one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a cheating division in this passage occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and its vowel pattern is unusual enough that the early grammarians wrote about it specifically. They record that the form is rare in Arabic generally, which is part of why the line lands: the wrongness of the arrangement is matched by the strangeness of the word chosen for it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates a name from a reality and puts the whole weight on the difference. What is denied is not that people worship these figures but that anything corresponds to the names. The two things followed instead are listed as distinct: conjecture, which is a failure of knowledge, and what the self wants, which is not. That pairing appears throughout the Quran, and it treats belief as governed by desire at least as much as by evidence.

crossReferences.why: Uses almost the same sentence about names inherited from fathers with no authority sent down.
Describes the face darkening at the news of a daughter, the valuation this argument borrows.
Describes a person who takes his own desire as his god, the second thing followed here.

studies.applyIt: Find one arrangement in your life where you have quietly kept the better half. The chores, the credit at work, the good chair, who gets the last word. You do not need to announce anything. Just swap it once this week and see whether it was as reasonable as it felt. The passage works by pointing at a split, not at a belief.

studies.title: How Many An Angel
studies.meaning: A short question closes the previous argument: does wanting something make it so. The answer is a statement about ownership that covers both ends of time, so the whole span is accounted for and nothing is left over for a wish to work on. Then the subject turns to angels, and the point is made by counting: however many there are, their intercession does nothing on its own. Permission comes first, and approval after it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The practical function of the shrines named a few lines earlier was intercession: offerings were made so that a figure closer to God would speak for the giver. The commentators read this passage as addressing that transaction directly rather than the question of whether angels exist, which nobody in the audience denied. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A verb for wanting something that is not in your hands, distinct from the words for asking or intending. It names the appetite itself, without any implication that action follows.
From a root meaning to make something even by adding a second, so an intercessor is a person who joins himself to your case. The image is of pairing rather than of pleading.
A second condition added after permission, from a root for being pleased and satisfied. Two separate approvals are required, one for the intercessor to speak and one for the case being made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Getting anything done in Arabia meant finding someone to speak for you. A stranger needed a protector to enter a town safely, a debtor needed a respected man to negotiate terms, a killer's family needed a mediator. The whole social order ran on people joining themselves to other people's cases. Religion worked the same way, which is why the passage does not argue against the practice but places a condition in front of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the word for intercession is the same one that gives Arabic its word for even numbers, as opposed to odd. An intercessor makes a single petitioner into a pair. The Quran uses both senses, and the connection means that intercession is described not as influence but as accompaniment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Intercession is affirmed and then placed entirely under permission, which preserves two things at once: that help is real, and that it is never independent. The double condition is the load-bearing part. Permission decides who may speak and approval decides whether the case stands, so no relationship with an intermediary can produce an outcome by itself. What is removed is not hope but leverage.

crossReferences.why: Says the angels do not intercede except for whom God approves, and stand in awe.
States the same double condition, permission to speak and acceptance of the word.
Swears by the even and the odd, using the same root that gives the word for intercession.

studies.applyIt: Think about who you would ask to speak for you if you were in serious trouble, and notice how quickly a name arrives. Everyone has a mental list of people whose word carries. Then ask whether you are on anyone else's list, and whether you have used that standing lately for someone who could not ask you directly.

studies.title: Conjecture Against The Truth
studies.meaning: A diagnosis and then an instruction. The naming of angels is traced to a specific absence: no knowledge, so conjecture fills the gap, and the passage adds a general rule about what conjecture is worth when truth is the question. Then the instruction, which is not to argue harder but to turn away, and the person to turn from is described by two things: he has turned from the reminder, and he wants only the present life.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators connect this passage to the same practice addressed a few lines earlier and note the causal claim it makes: the naming is traced to disbelief in the hereafter rather than to ignorance about angels. The instruction to turn away belongs to the Meccan period, when the community was small and argument with the leadership had reached its limit. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A word covering everything between doubt and near-certainty, so it is not the opposite of knowledge but a weaker grade of it. What the passage rejects is using that grade where certainty is needed.

To present your side rather than your face, a physical image of withdrawal without hostility. The word for what the other person did is different, a full turning of the back, so the two withdrawals are not described identically.
A noun that covers both the act of remembering and the thing remembered, so it names the Quran and the practice of reciting it at once. The English needs two words to keep both.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Withdrawing from an argument had a recognised social form. In a society where disputes were public and settled by standing, a man who stopped engaging was making a statement everyone could read, and it was not the same as conceding. Turning the shoulder was a gesture with meaning. The instruction here uses that vocabulary, and it assumes an audience who understood exactly what it looked like.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for conjecture appears three times in the space of six lines here, first as what the shrine names rest on and then twice in a single ayah, once as what is followed and once as what cannot substitute for truth. The repetition is the argument: the same word is put on both sides of the ledger.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established. The first is that a religious claim can be assessed by its evidential grade, and that a strong feeling about something is not a reason to hold it. The second is more surprising: the passage does not ask for more argument. It gives an instruction to withdraw, which means the Quran does not treat persuasion as unlimited. There is a point at which a person's own preference has become the whole of the matter.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule that conjecture is no substitute for the truth, in almost identical wording.
Describes the same naming of angels and asks whether the namers witnessed their creation.
Gives a related instruction, not to let the eyes pass beyond those who call on their Lord.

studies.applyIt: There is probably one conversation you keep restarting with someone who has made up their mind. Count how many times you have had it. This passage does not tell you to win it or to concede; it tells you to stop having it. Let the next opening go by unanswered once, and notice what you do with the energy you get back.

studies.title: The Reach Of Their Knowledge
studies.meaning: One sentence about the limits of a mind and one about the limits of a judgement. The first clause measures how far the knowledge of the people just described actually extends, and the word used is the one for the end of a journey: this is as far as they got. Then the sentence hands the assessment over. Twice it says your Lord knows better, once about the one who strayed and once about the one who found the way.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the argument about the shrines and the naming of angels. The commentators note the placement: the previous ayah tells the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to withdraw from a particular kind of opponent, and this one immediately removes any sense that withdrawing means passing judgement. No specific occasion is reported. It is read as a general limit on what any person may conclude about another.

keyTerms.note: A noun of place from the verb for arriving, so it names the point a traveller got to. Applied to knowledge it measures a distance rather than describing a quality.
A comparative form, so it says more knowing rather than all-knowing. Used twice in one line, it puts God's assessment above the reader's without saying the reader knows nothing.
A reflexive form, so the person is described as accepting direction rather than as being moved. The pairing with straying keeps both outcomes on the same grammatical footing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Desert travel gave the language its picture of a person's limit. A traveller had a stage he could reach before water ran out, and the distance was known and spoken about: this well, not the next one. Guides were judged by knowing exactly where a party could get to. The word this ayah uses for how far someone's knowledge goes belongs to that vocabulary of stages and reachable points.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparative for knowing better appears four times in three consecutive ayat here, twice in this line and twice in the one after next. In each case the subject is God and the object is a person's inner state. The surah spends its harshest passage insisting, four times over, that the final assessment is not being handed to the listener.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah does two things that pull in different directions and keeps both. It states plainly that some people have reached the end of what they are going to understand, which is a hard judgement. And then it removes the identification of who those people are from anyone but God. What is left for a reader is the disposition rather than the verdict: you may know that the category exists and not know who is in it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same sentence almost word for word about who strays and who is guided.
Uses the same formula in another Meccan surah, immediately after a defence of the messenger.
Says each acts according to his own manner, and your Lord knows who is better guided.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person you have privately written off and stop narrating them for a week. No summary of what they are like, out loud or in your head. You are not being asked to change your assessment, only to notice how often you produce it. This ayah does not say your reading is wrong. It says it is not the one that counts.

studies.title: Repaid With The Best
studies.meaning: The ayah gives a reason for ownership. Everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to God, and the purpose clause that follows says what the ownership is for: so that both kinds of people can be repaid. Then the two repayments are worded differently. Those who did badly are repaid by what they did, matched exactly. Those who did well are repaid with the best, which is a word that exceeds the deed rather than matching it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the passage where the surah moves from arguing about idols to stating how the world is settled. The commentators note the asymmetry in the two halves of the ayah and treat it as deliberate rather than stylistic. No specific occasion is reported. The line prepares the description of the people who will receive that better repayment, which follows immediately.

keyTerms.note: A verb from the root for what is bad or ugly, describing the doing rather than the doer. The Quran uses it of actions instead of labelling a person, which the grammar of the ayah preserves.
From the root for beauty and excellence, so doing good and doing something well are the same word. It names quality of action, not merely correctness of it.
A superlative from the same root as the verb just before it, so the reward is named with the word for the deed, raised a degree. Commentators read it as the garden and as something beyond it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Settlement of accounts was a public procedure. At the end of a season, partners in a caravan or a harvest sat down and worked out shares, and the arithmetic was expected to be exact in both directions. A man who took a fraction more than his due was remembered for it. Against that background, a reckoning that pays one side precisely and the other side more than precisely was a noticeable departure from the norm.
studies.didYouKnow: Both halves of this ayah use the same verb for repayment and the same preposition, and the difference is entirely in what follows it. One is repaid by what they did; the other is repaid by the best. The record is named in one clause and replaced in the other, and nothing else in the sentence changes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ownership is given a purpose here, which is unusual. The ayah does not say the world belongs to God and stop; it says it belongs to Him in order that people can be repaid, so possession is stated as the condition for justice rather than as a fact about power. And the asymmetry between the two settlements is where mercy enters without any word for mercy being used. Exactness on one side, more than exactness on the other.

crossReferences.why: Puts the arithmetic explicitly: a good deed counts tenfold and a bad one is matched exactly.
Names the same best reward and adds more on top of it, for those who did well.
States the principle as a question: is the reward for doing well anything but doing well.

studies.applyIt: Do one thing today better than it needs to be done. Not more of it, better: the email that could be two lines and is worth four, the meal, the apology. This ayah pays exactness for exactness and something more for quality, and quality is a decision you make in the last ten per cent of a task.

studies.title: Do Not Claim Your Own Purity
studies.meaning: The people just promised the better repayment are described, and the description is a subtraction: they keep clear of the major wrongs, with an exception the commentators discuss at length for the small lapses that everyone has. Then the ayah widens. God has known you since He raised you from the earth and while you were unformed in your mothers, which is offered as the reason for the instruction that closes it: do not certify yourselves.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators record several readings of the word for the excepted lapses, ranging from small sins to a fault approached and not committed, and they preserve the range rather than fixing it. The closing instruction is reported as having been directed at people in the early community who spoke of their own record, and the sources treat it as general rather than aimed at anyone in particular.

keyTerms.note: From a root for touching lightly or passing close to something. The commentators read it as minor slips, or as approaching a fault without falling into it, and both readings are transmitted.
The first word means wide or roomy, used of open ground and of ample means. Forgiveness is described as an area rather than an act, so the image is of space to fit things into.
From a root for growth and for purification, the same one behind the word for the purifying due on wealth. Applied to oneself it means issuing a certificate nobody asked you for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Self-praise had a formal place in Arabian life. Boasting contests were a recognised genre, a man recited his own lineage and deeds before a gathering, and a well-made boast was a serious social asset. The poetry is full of it. An instruction not to declare your own record clean cut against a practice the audience regarded as accomplishment rather than as vanity, which is why it needed stating at all.
studies.didYouKnow: This single ayah names two moments before a person could remember anything: when they were brought out of the earth, and when they were unformed inside their mothers. Both are offered as evidence in an argument about self-assessment. The reasoning is that a witness who was present before you existed has a longer record of you than you have.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The instruction against certifying yourself is grounded in an argument about evidence rather than in a call to modesty. You do not have the file. Someone who watched the whole of your making has it, which makes self-assessment a question of access before it is a question of humility. And the exception for small lapses sits inside the same ayah as the vastness of forgiveness, so the standard being described is high and the tolerance around it is wide.

crossReferences.why: Names the same act directly, of people who declare themselves pure, and says God purifies whom He wills.
Describes those who avoid the major wrongs and forgive when they are angry.
Gives the same sequence at length, dust then a drop then a formed shape in the womb.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you slip a small piece of self-certification into a conversation — I always, I would never, I am not the kind of person who. Everyone does it and nobody hears themselves do it. Catch one this week and let the sentence stop before the claim. The silence afterwards is uncomfortable and instructive.

studies.title: He Gave A Little And Stopped
studies.meaning: A portrait in two verbs. He turned away, and then he gave a small amount and dried up, which is the literal sense of the second verb: a well that yields and then hits rock. The questions that follow ask where his confidence came from, since stopping implies knowing the account is settled. Then two sources are named, the scrolls of Moses and Abraham, and Abraham is described with one word: he fulfilled.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators report an occasion for these lines involving a man who had agreed to take on another person's burden in exchange for payment, gave part of what he promised and then withheld the rest. They differ over who he was and some keep the passage general. What is not disputed is the pattern being described: a transfer of responsibility purchased and then abandoned halfway.

keyTerms.note: From a verb used of a digger who strikes hard rock and abandons the well. It describes giving that ends because the giver decided it had, not because there was nothing left.
The plural of a word for a sheet or leaf of writing material. It is used of earlier revelations and of the records opened at the reckoning, so the same word covers scripture and ledger.
An intensive form of the verb for paying in full. The object is left out, so the sentence says he completed without saying what, and the commentators supply everything he was tested with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Digging a well was the largest investment a group could make. Men worked down through soil and gravel for days, and hitting a stratum they could not cut through meant the whole effort was lost and the hole abandoned. Half-dug wells were a familiar sight and a byword for wasted work. The verb used for this man's giving comes straight from that experience, and everyone hearing it saw the abandoned shaft.
studies.didYouKnow: The scrolls of Moses and Abraham are mentioned in only two places in the Quran, here and at the end of surah 87, and both times they are cited for content rather than described. In neither case is the reader told anything about what the scrolls looked like or how they survived, only what was in them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats a stopped act of generosity as a claim about knowledge. To decide you have given enough is to know where the line is, and the questions put to the man ask exactly that: do you have the unseen, so that you can see. Nobody thinks of it that way, which is the point. Then the alternative source is named, and it is not private insight but something written down and available.

crossReferences.why: Names the same two sets of scrolls, in the reverse order, at the close of that surah.
Describes Abraham being tested with words and completing them, the fulfilment named here.
Describes a man who gathered and hoarded, the same holding back seen from the other side.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you started giving and quietly stopped: money, time, attention to a person who needed it. Do not restart the whole arrangement. Give one instalment of it this week, the smallest version, and notice whether the reason you stopped was that you ran out or that you decided you had done enough.

studies.title: Only What You Walked Toward
studies.meaning: Five clauses, each opening the same way, forming a list of what was in the earlier scriptures. Responsibility is individual: nobody carries another's load. What a person owns is what he worked at, not what he inherited or intended. That effort will be seen, then repaid in full, using a word that means completed rather than generous. The last clause stops the chain at its endpoint, which is not a place but a Lord.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah whose second half turns on what was written in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham. The passage answers a specific Meccan attitude reported in the surah just before, a man who paid a little and then stopped, apparently believing another person could carry his account. Arab society ran on collective liability, so an insistence on individual responsibility cut against ordinary assumptions.

keyTerms.note: The verb and the noun beside it come from the same root, which names a load carried on the back and also a minister who shoulders a king's work. The image is weight, not guilt.

A verb of walking quickly and of exerting oneself toward something. It describes movement rather than result, which is why the classical readers stress that what is owned is the effort, not the achievement.
A superlative from a root meaning to pay in full and to keep a promise. The word does not mean generous; it means nothing withheld, which cuts both ways in a passage about repayment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Arabia a man's debts, feuds and honour belonged to his clan. Blood money was collected across a whole kin group, and a killing by one member could be paid for by cousins who had never met the victim. That system held society together and also meant nobody stood alone. These ayat describe a reckoning where the clan does not attend, which would have sounded less comforting then than it does now.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about one soul not carrying another's load appears five times in the Quran, in five different surahs, always in the same wording. Repetition at that level is rare. Here it is presented not as a new statement but as a quotation, part of what the passage says was already written in the scrolls of Moses and Abraham.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage builds a small system of accountability. Nobody can be charged for another; nobody can bank on another's credit; the record is effort rather than outcome; the settlement is exact; and the whole thing terminates in God rather than in a state or a balance. Read together, these remove both the fear of inherited fault and the hope of inherited merit, which is a harder combination than it first appears.

crossReferences.why: Carries the identical clause about burdens and ends, like this passage, with the return to God.
Dramatises the same rule, showing someone overloaded calling for help and finding nothing transferred.
Gives the same seeing of one's own work at the finest possible resolution, down to an atom's weight.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have been waiting to feel ready for, and do fifteen minutes of it today. Not the whole thing. This passage measures what you move toward, not what you complete, and fifteen minutes is a real quantity of striving. Put it in the calendar for tomorrow before you finish today's.

studies.title: Laughter, Weeping, Death, Life
studies.meaning: A run of short statements, each attributing something to God, and the pairings are the argument. Laughing and weeping are put beside dying and living, which places an emotion in the same category as an event: neither is something a person produces. Then the making of the pair, male and female, is traced back to a drop, and the sequence closes by saying that the second bringing into existence is upon Him, which is the language of an obligation He has taken on.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, inside the long list of statements that closes this surah, each introduced the same way. The commentators read the list as the content of what was in the earlier scrolls, continuing from the reference to Moses and Abraham a few lines earlier. No occasion is reported for these particular ayat, and the classical works treat the whole run as one connected passage.

keyTerms.note: A causative of the ordinary verb for laughing. Attributing the cause of laughter to God, rather than the occasion for it, is what makes the line unexpected in a list otherwise about life and death.
A word for the last of the water in a vessel or a drop left in a bucket. It is chosen for smallness rather than for biology, which is how the contrast with a whole person is made.
A noun for raising or originating something, with an adjective meaning other. The phrase names resurrection as a repeat of an act already performed once, which is the argument compressed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grief and joy were public and organised in Arabia. Professional mourners were hired for a death, and their weeping was a service with a price; celebration at a birth or a return was equally communal. Nobody in that society thought of laughter or tears as private states. Attributing both to God spoke to an audience who already experienced them as things that happen to a community rather than inside one person.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for causing laughter appears in this form only here in the Quran, and it is the only place laughter is attributed to God as something He brings about. Everywhere else in the Quran laughing is something people do, and several of those places describe laughing at somebody else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing laughter and tears in a list with life and death makes a claim most people resist: that your inner weather is not yours to arrange. It does not say emotions are unreal or that they should be suppressed, only that their origin is not where you assume. And then the list moves to the second creation and calls it something incumbent, so the return is presented as a commitment rather than as a display of power.

crossReferences.why: Uses a matching phrase for the later bringing forth, telling the reader to travel and look at the first.
Runs the same argument from the drop to the second creation, and asks why you do not remember.
Uses laughing and weeping as a matched pair, in a reversal of what a life earned.

studies.applyIt: Think back to the last time you laughed properly, the kind you did not choose. You could not have produced it on purpose and you will not be able to schedule the next one. This passage puts that in the same sentence as being alive. Notice the next one when it arrives, and let it be a thing you received rather than a thing you did.

studies.title: He Enriched And He Gave
studies.meaning: The list continues and turns to property. Two verbs that rhyme and differ by one letter, one meaning to make rich and the other read by the commentators as giving possessions to keep, so wealth and the holding of it are both traced to the same source. Then a star is named, and the commentators explain that some Arabs worshipped it. The last three lines list peoples who were removed, and the destruction is attributed as directly as the enrichment was.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The star named here was an object of veneration among some Arabian groups, and the commentators identify particular tribes associated with the practice. Naming it inside a list of God's acts placed it as a created thing with a Lord. The three peoples that follow were the standard examples of destroyed nations, and the phrase for the first of them distinguishes an earlier group from a later one.

keyTerms.note: From a root for acquiring and keeping property, which also gives the word for livestock held as capital. Commentators read it as granting what a person keeps, as distinct from what passes through his hands.

The name of the brightest star in the night sky, used in Arabic without explanation. Calling God its Lord answers a specific practice without describing it, which is how the surah handles the other shrines too.
From the root for remaining and lasting, in a form meaning to leave something over. Negated, it says nothing was left, and the same root supplies the Quran's word for what endures.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in that world came in two forms and people distinguished them carefully. There was what moved — trade goods, coin, what a caravan returned with — and there was what stayed, meaning camels, palms and a well. A man could be rich for a season and own nothing durable. The two verbs opening this passage map onto that distinction, and the audience heard the difference immediately.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only place in the Quran where a particular star is named. Elsewhere stars are referred to as a class, or sworn by without identification, but here one is singled out and given a Lord. The surah that opens with an oath by an unnamed star closes by naming the brightest one there is.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attributes wealth and its loss, life and its ending, to one source, and it does so without moralising about any of them. Nobody in the list of destroyed peoples is described as poor and nobody enriched is described as good. What is being established is not a moral economy but a single agency, which is a harder claim, because it leaves the reader without a rule connecting circumstance to worth.

crossReferences.why: Names the stars as marks for finding the way by land and sea, given for navigation.
States the same attribution of honour and abasement, giving and withholding, as a single act.
Lists the same destroyed peoples and describes what your Lord did to each of them.

studies.applyIt: Split what you own into two lists tonight: what would still be there in five years and what will be gone by then. It takes ten minutes and most people find the second list is where their attention lives. You are not being asked to give anything away. Just look at the proportion, and see whether it matches what you would have guessed.

studies.title: Which Of These Do You Doubt
studies.meaning: The overturned towns are named with a word that describes what happened to them rather than where they were, and what covered them is left unstated in the same construction used earlier for the tree. Then the list stops and asks a question, and the question is not about denial but about doubt. The last two lines close the surah's argument: this is a warning of the same kind as earlier warnings, and the thing that draws near has drawn near.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The overturned towns are the settlements of Lot's people, on the trade road north, and the Meccan audience passed the region on the Syrian route. The commentators note that the surah has now moved from the near past of Aad and Thamud to a site the listeners knew, and then to a question addressed to them directly. No occasion is reported for these lines.

keyTerms.note: A participle from a verb meaning to be turned upside down, so the name is the event. The Quran uses this description in three places and never gives the settlement a proper name.
A plural for gifts and blessings, and the same word carries the refrain that runs through the surah after this one. Here it is paired with doubting rather than with denying.
An active participle from a verb for a time drawing close, used of a departure that is nearly due. It names the Hour by its nearness rather than by anything that happens in it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan's departure was announced in stages. Word went round that the company would leave, then that it would leave soon, then that the loading had started, and a man with business to settle had a shrinking window he could feel. The word this passage uses for the Hour comes from that vocabulary of imminence, and everybody in the audience had experienced the particular pressure it names.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for favours in the question here is the same word that carries the famous refrain of the following surah, where it is repeated thirty-one times. Outside that surah the noun occurs exactly once in the whole Quran, and this is it. There the question is which favours you deny; here it is which of them you doubt.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The question at the centre of this passage asks about doubt rather than about rejection, which is a different accusation and a gentler one. It allows for a listener who has not decided. And the line that follows places the warning in a series: this is one of the earlier warnings, not a new kind of message, so the claim being made is about continuity rather than novelty. Then the surah stops arguing.

crossReferences.why: Begins the refrain built on the same word for favours, asking which of them you deny.
Uses the same name for the Hour, warning of the day of the imminent thing.
Lists the overturned towns among the peoples whose news should have reached them.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between what you deny and what you doubt. Denial is a position and doubt is a weather system, and most people have far more of the second than they admit. Name one thing this week that you have been treating as settled and are actually unsure about. Say it once, to yourself or to somebody. Nothing needs to follow.

studies.title: Laughing And Not Weeping
studies.meaning: Four short lines and then an instruction. The first asks whether this account is what they find amazing, using the word for a report or a piece of news, and the next two put laughing and not weeping side by side as a single behaviour rather than two. The last description before the instruction is a word the commentators explain in several ways, all of them about being absorbed in something that does not matter. Then the surah ends with a prostration.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the sources report that when this surah was first recited publicly at the sanctuary, those present prostrated at its final line, including people who had not accepted the message. The report is transmitted in the classical collections and the commentators cite it when discussing the surah's ending. The final ayah is one of the places in the Quran marked for prostration in recitation.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for talk or news, used here of the Quran itself. Calling it a report rather than a scripture matches the challenge earlier in the surah before this one.
A rare participle the commentators gloss as being distracted, singing, playing, or standing about proudly. They preserve the range, and every reading shares the sense of attention spent on nothing.
The verb for putting the forehead to the ground, the lowest physical position a person can take. It arrives with no preparation, as the answer to four lines about standing around.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary at Mecca was a public space and recitation there happened in front of everyone: traders, pilgrims, the leadership, people passing through. Nothing was private. A gathering that stood listening and then went down together would have been visible across the whole enclosure, and the sources treat the moment as remarkable precisely because of who was standing there when it happened.
studies.didYouKnow: The rare word in the second-to-last line of this surah occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and the classical commentators list four or five different meanings for it without settling on one. It is the last thing the surah says about the listeners before it tells them to prostrate, and nobody is entirely certain what it accuses them of.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah has spent sixty lines on argument and ends by asking for a body position. Nothing is added to the case; the instruction simply follows. That order says something about what the arguing was for, since the passage does not conclude with a proposition to accept but with something to do. And the two lines before it treat amusement as the opposite of worship, which is a more interesting opposition than disbelief would have been.

crossReferences.why: Asks a similar question about this account, and about making denial your daily provision.
Describes people falling on their faces weeping when the recitation is read to them.
Closes another Meccan surah with the same instruction to prostrate and draw near.

studies.applyIt: Read the last line of this surah out loud and then sit for ten seconds without doing anything else. The chapter spends sixty lines arguing and ends with a physical act rather than a conclusion. Notice how strongly you want to keep thinking about it instead. That wanting is close to what the second-to-last line describes.
